title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXXIV: The Sorrow of Hrethel (lines 2391–2459)
part: Fitt XXXIV · The Sorrow of Hrethel (lines 2391–2459)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 90–92, lines 2391–2459 (fitt XXXIV). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.l: He remembered the requital for the people-fall in later days, became to Eadgils, to the destitute one, a friend;
sentences.i: In later days he kept in mind the repayment owed for his prince’s fall, and became a friend to Eadgils in his destitution;
sentences.n: ‘Sē’ is Beowulf, who has just been made ruler of the Geats (2389–2390), and the sentence is built on two verbs, ‘gemunde’ (‘remembered’, with ‘lēan’ as its object) and ‘wearð’ (‘became’), with the friend as predicate noun and the befriended man, ‘Ēadgilse fēasceaftum’, in the dative. ‘ðæs lēodhryres’ is a genitive depending on ‘lēan’, ‘the requital for that fall’. ‘lēodhryre’ is ‘people-fall’ (‘lēod’ ‘man, prince, people’ + ‘hryre’ ‘fall’); the fall meant is Heardred’s (‘Heardrēd læg’, 2388), the young king Beowulf served. ‘lēan’ is ‘requital’, the payback a debt of vengeance calls for. ‘uferan dōgrum’ is a dative, ‘in later days’. ‘fēasceaft’ (‘destitute’) is the word the Prologue used of the foundling Scyld; Eadgils is the Swedish prince, son of Ohthere, who came over the sea as an exile (2380). This is the Fitt’s opening: Klaeber prints the section number XXXIIII at 2391.

sentences.l: with a folk he raised up, over the wide sea, the son of Ohthere, with warriors and weapons;
sentences.i: He supported the son of Ohthere across the wide sea with a host, with men and weapons;
sentences.n: The object is ‘sunu Ōhteres’ (accusative), Eadgils again, and ‘folce’ is a dative of means, ‘with a host’. ‘gestēpte’ I take as ‘raised up, exalted’ (lexica, from the verb ‘stēpan’), which in this setting must mean ‘set on his feet, aided’; that sense is a guess from context, since the verb is rare. ‘ofer sǣ sīde’ is ‘over the wide sea’, with ‘sīde’ a feminine accusative agreeing with ‘sǣ’; Schröder and Schücking read the two words as one compound, ‘sǣsīðe’ (‘sea-journey’, with ‘ð’), which would change the construction. ‘wigum’ with short ‘i’ is the dative plural of ‘wiga’, ‘warrior’ (‘wīg’ ‘battle’ would have a long vowel), so ‘warriors and weapons’ is a pair.

sentences.t:
hē gewræc syððan
cealdum cearsīðum, cyning ealdre binēat.
sentences.l: he avenged it afterwards with cold sorrow-journeys, deprived the king of life.
sentences.i: Afterwards he took vengeance, by cold and sorrowful marches, and robbed the king of his life.
sentences.n: ‘gewræc’ (‘avenged’) has no object; ‘it’ is the fall of Heardred. ‘hē’ is ambiguous: it may be Beowulf, the subject so far, or Eadgils, the nearest man named (‘sunu Ōhteres’); the next sentence names Beowulf afresh (‘sunu Ecgðīowes’), which favours Eadgils as the avenger. I leave ‘he’ unresolved in both lines. ‘cealdum cearsīðum’ is an instrumental, ‘by cold sorrow-journeys’ (‘cearu’ ‘sorrow’ + ‘sīð’ ‘journey’): grim expeditions, ‘cold’ in the sense of cheerless; the exact sense is a reading, not a given. The apparatus lists two alternatives: ‘cealde cearsīðas’ (an accusative, ‘cold sorrow-journeys’ as what he avenged; the siglum is ‘Aant.’) and ‘cwealm cearsīðum’ (Trautmann). ‘binēat’ is the preterite of ‘benēotan’, ‘deprive’, with the king as object and ‘ealdre’ (dative of ‘ealdor’ ‘life’) the thing taken. The king is the Swedish one, Ongentheow’s son (2387), who went home when Heardred fell.

sentences.t:
Swā hē nīða gehwane genesen hæfde,
slīðra geslyhta, sunu Ecgðīowes,
ellenweorca, oð ðone ānne dæg,
þē hē wið þām wyrme gewegan sceolde.
sentences.l: So he, every one of the hostilities, had come through, of cruel clashes, the son of Ecgtheow, of courage-works, until that one day on which he had to fight against the worm.
sentences.i: So the son of Ecgtheow had come safely through every battle, every cruel clash, every feat of courage, until the one day when he had to fight the dragon.
sentences.n: The pluperfect ‘genesen hæfde’ (‘had come through’) takes its object ‘nīða gehwane’ (accusative, ‘each of the hostilities’), and two genitives in variation follow, ‘slīðra geslyhta’ (‘of cruel clashes’, ‘geslyht’ a blow or fray) and ‘ellenweorca’ (‘of deeds of courage’, ‘ellen’ ‘courage’ + ‘weorc’ ‘work’): the same thing named three times, a catalogue of battles. ‘sunu Ecgðīowes’ is Beowulf, the subject of ‘hæfde’ named at last. ‘oð ðone ānne dæg’ is ‘until that one day’, and ‘þē’ is the relative ‘on which’. ‘gewegan’ I take to mean ‘to fight it out’ (the root verb is ‘bear’, so ‘carry through’); the lexica give both senses, and the sense ‘fight’ suits ‘wið’. ‘wyrm’ is the house ‘worm’ in the literal line and ‘dragon’ in the idiomatic one.

sentences.t:
Gewāt þā twelfa sum torne gebolgen
dryhten Gēata dracan scēawian;
sentences.l: Went then, as one of twelve, swollen with anger, the lord of the Geats to look upon the dragon;
sentences.i: Then the lord of the Geats went, with eleven companions, swollen with anger, to see the dragon;
sentences.n: ‘Gewāt’ (‘went’) is the verb, ‘dryhten Gēata’ its subject delayed to the end, and ‘dracan scēawian’ an infinitive of purpose, ‘to look upon the dragon’ (‘dracan’ accusative). ‘twelfa sum’ is the idiom for ‘one of twelve’: ‘twelfa’ is the genitive plural of ‘twelf’ (‘of twelve’) and ‘sum’ is ‘one’; Beowulf counts himself, so eleven men go with him (the thirteenth comes in the next lines). The manuscript writes the number as a numeral, ‘.xiia.’ (the apparatus), which Klaeber spells out. ‘torne gebolgen’ is ‘swollen with wrath’ (‘torn’ dative ‘anger’, ‘gebolgen’ past participle of ‘belgan’, the swelling of a man’s body with rage). The cause of the anger is in the preceding Fitt: the dragon has burned his hall.

sentences.t:
hæfde þā gefrūnen, hwanan sīo fǣhð ārās,
bealonīð biorna;
sentences.l: He had then learned by asking whence the feud arose, the bale-malice of men;
sentences.i: By then he had learned where the feud had come from, the baleful malice that threatened men;
sentences.n: ‘hæfde gefrūnen’ is a pluperfect of ‘gefrignan’ (‘learn by asking’), and ‘hwanan’ opens an indirect question, ‘from where the feud arose’ (‘sīo fǣhð’ nominative). ‘bealonīð’ (‘bale-malice’, the rendering the earlier part gave it) stands in apposition to ‘fǣhð’. ‘biorna’ is a genitive plural, ‘of men’ (‘beorn’ a poetic word for man), and what it hangs on is not settled: I take it as ‘malice against men’, which I have rendered loosely in the idiomatic line; ‘malice of men’ is the strict reading and leaves open whose malice is meant. The apparatus adds that the Thorkelin transcripts place the start of folio 183b at ‘cwōm’, in the next unit.

sentences.t:
him tō bearme cwōm
māðþụmfæt mǣre þurh ðæs meldan hond.
sentences.l: to him into the lap came a famous treasure-vessel through the informer’s hand.
sentences.i: A famous cup of treasure came into his keeping, through the hand of the informer.
sentences.n: ‘him tō bearme cwōm’ is ‘to him into the lap came’, ‘bearm’ being the lap or bosom, that is, into his keeping; ‘cwōm’ is a variant of ‘cōm’. The subject follows: ‘māðþumfæt mǣre’, a famous ‘treasure-vessel’ (‘māðþum’ ‘treasure’ + ‘fæt’ ‘vessel’), presumably the cup carried off from the dragon’s hoard. The dot under the ‘u’ in ‘māðþụmfæt’ is Klaeber’s sign that this vowel does not count in the metre; the first one this part meets, and there are more (baldọr, symbẹl, morþọrbed, ǣnịgum). ‘ðæs meldan hond’ is ‘the informer’s hand’ (‘melda’ a weak noun from ‘meldian’ ‘announce, inform’): the man who showed the way is described in the next line.

sentences.t:
Sē wæs on ðām ðrēate þreottēoða secg,
sē ðæs orleges ōr onstealde,
hæft hygegiōmor, sceolde hēan ðonon
wong wīsian.
sentences.l: He was in that troop the thirteenth man, he who the beginning of the strife set up, a captive, sad-minded; he had to, abject, point out the plain from there.
sentences.i: He was the thirteenth man of that company, the one who had set the strife going, a captive now, heavy at heart, and wretched as he was, he had to show them the place from there.
sentences.n: ‘þreottēoða secg’ is ‘the thirteenth man’ (an ordinal, ‘þreottēoða’), the informer added to Beowulf’s twelve. ‘sē ðæs orleges ōr onstealde’ is a relative clause, ‘he who established the beginning of the strife’ (‘ōr’ ‘beginning’, ‘orleges’ genitive of ‘orleg’ ‘strife, war’, ‘onstellan’ ‘set up, begin’): by taking the cup he roused the dragon. ‘hæft’ is a noun, ‘captive’, in apposition to ‘sē’, and ‘hygegiōmor’ is ‘mind-sad’ (‘hyge’ ‘mind’ + ‘geōmor’ ‘sad’). ‘sceolde’ is ‘had to’, with ‘hēan’ ‘abject’ (a different word from ‘hēah’ ‘high’) and the infinitive ‘wīsian’ (‘direct, point out’) taking ‘wong’ (‘plain, ground’) as object. What ‘ðonon’ (‘from there’) looks back to is not shown. ‘Plain’ here is the open ground where the barrow lies, so ‘show the place’ is the sense; that is an inference.

sentences.t:
Hē ofer willan gīong
tō ðæs ðe hē eorðsele ānne wisse,
hlǣw under hrūsan holmwylme nēh,
ȳðgewinne;
sentences.l: He went against his will to where he knew a certain earth-hall, a barrow under the ground, near the sea-surge, the wave-strife;
sentences.i: Against his will he went on, to the place where he knew of a certain earth-hall, a barrow beneath the ground, close by the surge of the sea and the strife of the waves;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is the informer, the thirteenth man of the unit before, not Beowulf. ‘Hē ofer willan gīong’ is ‘he went beyond (against) his will’; ‘ofer’ with the accusative ‘willan’ is the idiom for ‘unwillingly’. ‘tō ðæs ðe’ is a conjunction, ‘to the place where’ (literally ‘to that which’), and ‘wisse’ is ‘knew’ (‘witan’). ‘eorðsele ānne’ is ‘a certain earth-hall’ (‘eorðe’ ‘earth’ + ‘sele’ ‘hall’; ‘ānne’ may also be ‘one, sole’), a compound explained by ‘hlǣw under hrūsan’, ‘barrow under the ground’. ‘holmwylme nēh’ is ‘near the sea-surge’ (‘holm’ ‘sea’ + ‘wylm’ ‘surge’; ‘nēh’ takes the dative), and ‘ȳðgewinne’ is a second dative in variation, ‘wave-strife’ (‘ȳð’ ‘wave’ + ‘gewinn’ ‘strife’): the sea breaking at the foot of the headland.

sentences.t:
sē wæs innan full
wrǣtta ond wīra.
sentences.l: it was inside full of ornaments and of wires.
sentences.i: Inside it was full of ornaments and wire.
sentences.n: ‘sē’ is the masculine pronoun for the barrow, ‘it’; ‘innan’ is ‘inside’, and ‘full’ takes the genitive, so ‘wrǣtta ond wīra’ are ‘of ornaments and of wires’. ‘wrǣt’ is a piece of fine workmanship, an ornament, and ‘wīr’ is wire, here the twisted metal-work set in jewelry; I have kept ‘wire’ rather than guess at a finer sense. The line only lists what the barrow holds.

sentences.l: A guardian, monstrous, a ready war-fighter, held the gold-treasures, old, under the earth;
sentences.i: A monstrous guardian, a fighter ready for battle, kept the gold-treasures, old as he was, beneath the earth;
sentences.n: ‘Weard’ is a noun, nominative, ‘guardian’, and the rest of the sentence unpacks it: ‘unhīore’ (‘monstrous’, the word an earlier part spelled ‘unhȳre’) and ‘gearo gūðfreca’ (‘ready war-fighter’, ‘freca’ ‘bold one, warrior’), all describing the dragon without naming it. ‘goldmāðmas hēold’ is ‘held the gold-treasures’ (‘goldmāðm’ ‘gold-treasure’, accusative plural), and ‘eald’ is nominative singular, so it agrees with the guardian, not the gold: the creature is ancient. ‘under eorðan’ is ‘beneath the earth’.

sentences.t:
næs þæt ȳðe cēap
tō gegangenne gumena ǣnịgum.
sentences.l: that was not an easy bargain to be got by any of men.
sentences.i: It was no easy bargain for any man to win.
sentences.n: ‘næs þæt ȳðe cēap’ is ‘that was not an easy bargain’; ‘ȳðe’ ‘easy’ is a different word from ‘ȳð’ ‘wave’ in ‘ȳðgewinne’ three lines earlier (2412). ‘cēap’ is ‘purchase, price’, and ‘tō gegangenne’ is an inflected infinitive, ‘to be got’ (‘gegangan’), with the dative ‘gumena ǣnịgum’, ‘for any of men’. The understatement ‘not easy’ means ‘almost impossible’, and ‘bargain’ makes the hoard a thing with a price. The dot under the ‘ị’ of ‘ǣnịgum’ is the metre sign again.

sentences.t: Gesæt ðā on næsse nīðheard cyning;
sentences.l: Sat down then on the headland the strife-hard king;
sentences.i: Then the king, hard in battle, sat down on the headland;
sentences.n: ‘Gesæt’ is the preterite of ‘gesittan’ (‘sat down, took a seat’), with ‘on næsse’ (‘on the headland’, dative) and the subject ‘cyning’ placed last with its adjective, ‘nīðheard’ (‘hard in hostility’, ‘nīð’ ‘strife, enmity’ + ‘heard’ ‘hard’). The headland is the one by which the barrow stands, ‘nīwe be næsse’ (2243), so Beowulf sits beside the barrow. What follows gives the king’s mood while he waits.

sentences.t:
þenden hǣlo ābēad heorðgenēatum,
goldwine Gēata.
sentences.l: while he proclaimed health to the hearth-companions, the gold-friend of the Geats.
sentences.i: while he bade farewell to his hearth-companions, the gold-friend of the Geats.
sentences.n: ‘þenden’ is ‘while’, and ‘hǣlo ābēad’ is ‘offered health’ (‘hǣlu’ accusative ‘health, good fortune’, ‘ābēodan’ ‘announce, offer’), the farewell of a leader to the men he leaves: ‘hail’ to them. ‘heorðgenēatum’ is the dative of ‘heorðgenēat’, ‘hearth-companion’ (‘heorð’ ‘hearth’ + ‘genēat’ ‘companion’), a retainer who shares the king’s fire and table. ‘goldwine Gēata’ is the house ‘gold-friend’, nominative, Beowulf again in apposition to the subject of ‘ābēad’. The ‘þenden’ clause belongs to ‘Gesæt’ in the previous unit; the next unit gives his state of mind.

sentences.t:
Him wæs geōmor sefa,
wǣfre ond wælfūs, wyrd ungemete nēah,
sē ðone gomelan grētan sceolde,
sēcean sāwle hord, sundur gedǣlan
līf wið līce;
sentences.l: To him was the mind mournful, wavering and death-ready, fate immeasurably near, which was to greet the aged one, seek the soul’s hoard, part asunder life from body;
sentences.i: His spirit was heavy within him, restless and ready for death, with fate immeasurably near: fate that was to meet the old man, to seek out the treasure of his soul, and sunder his life from his body;
sentences.n: ‘Him wæs geōmor sefa’ is a dative of possession, ‘to him was the mind sad’, then two adjectives in variation, ‘wǣfre’ (‘wavering, restless’) and ‘wælfūs’ (‘death-ready’, ‘wæl’ ‘the slain, slaughter’ + ‘fūs’ ‘eager, ready’): a man who feels his own end. ‘wyrd’ is fate, feminine, but the relative is ‘sē’, masculine; Grein and others read the feminine ‘sēo’; the masculine ‘sefa’ is also available as antecedent, but I take fate to be what greets the old man. The sentence ends in three infinitives with ‘sceolde’ (‘was to’): ‘grētan’ (‘greet, approach’, grimly), ‘sēcean’ and ‘gedǣlan’ (‘divide’), and ‘sundur’ means ‘asunder’. ‘sāwle hord’ is ‘the soul’s hoard’, which I take as the soul thought of as a treasure kept in the body; some take ‘hord’ as the body that holds the soul, and the line is uncertain. ‘līf wið līce’ is ‘life from body’.

sentences.t:
nō þon lange wæs
feorh æþelinges flǣsce bewunden.
sentences.l: Not for long by that was the prince’s life wound about with flesh.
sentences.i: It was not to be much longer that the prince’s life would be wrapped in flesh.
sentences.n: ‘nō þon lange’ is ‘not (by) that long’, ‘þon’ an instrumental, and the sense is ‘not much longer’; Grundtvig and, with a query, Sedgefield propose ‘þonne’, and Grein (first edition, with a query) ‘leng ne’; Klaeber’s text keeps ‘þon lange’. The verb ‘wæs’ is a preterite looking forward from the speaker’s knowledge, so I give ‘was not to be’ in the idiomatic line. ‘feorh’ is nominative, ‘æþelinges’ genitive, ‘flǣsce bewunden’ ‘wound about with flesh’ (a participle of ‘bewindan’): the body pictured as a garment wound round the life.

sentences.t: Bīowulf maþelade, bearn Ecgðēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: ‘maþelade’ is the weak-verb ending of ‘maþelode’, ‘spoke formally’, and ‘Bīowulf’ is the spelling Klaeber prints here of the name elsewhere written ‘Bēowulf’. What follows is a remembering. Klaeber prints no closing quotation mark by the end of this part, so the speech goes on into the next Fitt.

sentences.t:
‘Fela ic on giogoðe gūðrǣsa genæs,
orleghwīla;
sentences.l: ‘Many of war-rushes in youth I came through, of war-times;
sentences.i: ‘In my youth I came through many onslaughts, many a time of war;
sentences.n: ‘Fela’ takes the genitive, so ‘gūðrǣsa’ is ‘of war-rushes’ (‘gūðrǣs’ ‘battle-rush’, the house ‘war-rush’ and ‘onslaught’), and ‘genæs’ is the preterite of ‘genesan’ (‘come through, survive’). ‘orleghwīla’ is a second genitive plural in variation, ‘war-times’ (‘orleg’ ‘war’ + ‘hwīl’ ‘time’). ‘on giogoðe’ is ‘in youth’. The old king begins with his own record: the same ‘nīða gehwane genesen’ the narrator gave him, in his own mouth.

sentences.t: ic þæt eall gemon.
sentences.l: I remember all that.
sentences.i: I remember it all.
sentences.n: ‘gemon’ is the present of the preterite-present verb ‘gemunan’ (‘remember’), with ‘þæt eall’ as its object. It is the same verb as ‘gemunde’ at 2391 and ‘sibbe gemunde’ below, and the passive ‘gemyndgad’ at 2450 is built from the same root: memory runs through the whole passage, which moves from vengeance remembered to a grief that cannot be repaid.

sentences.t:
Ic wæs syfanwintre, þā mec sinca baldọr,
frēawine folca æt mīnum fæder genam;
sentences.l: I was seven winters old, when me the lord of treasures, the lord-friend of peoples, took from my father;
sentences.i: I was seven winters old when the lord of treasures, lord and friend of peoples, took me from my father;
sentences.n: ‘syfanwintre’ is ‘seven winters old’ (an adjective, ‘wintre’ ‘winters old’; Old English counts ages in winters). The subject of ‘genam’ (‘took’) is the pair ‘sinca baldọr’, ‘lord of treasures’ (‘sinc’ ‘treasure’ in the genitive plural; ‘baldor’ ‘lord, prince’), and ‘frēawine folca’, ‘lord-friend of peoples’ (‘frēawine’ ‘lord and friend’), both naming Hrethel, who comes by name in the next line. ‘æt mīnum fæder’ is ‘from my father’ (‘æt’ + dative), and ‘mec’ is the longer accusative of ‘ic’. The boy is placed in a kinsman’s court to be raised: Hrethel, Higelac’s father, is Beowulf’s grandfather. The dot under the ‘o’ of ‘baldọr’ is the metre sign.

sentences.t:
hēold mec ond hæfde Hrēðel cyning,
geaf mē sinc ond symbẹl, sibbe gemunde;
sentences.l: held me and had me King Hrethel, gave me treasure and feast, remembered kinship;
sentences.i: King Hrethel kept me and held me as his own, gave me treasure and feasting, and remembered that we were kin;
sentences.n: The subject, ‘Hrēðel cyning’ (Hrethel the king), is held back until after the first two verbs, ‘hēold mec ond hæfde’, ‘held me and had me’, which together mean ‘kept me as his own’. The apparatus records that Holthausen (first edition) and Sedgefield move the king’s name so that it follows ‘geaf mē’ (‘geaf mē Hrēðel cyning’), and that Holthausen’s later editions give ‘Hrēðel cyning geaf’, so that the king’s name goes with ‘geaf’ and not with ‘hēold … hæfde’; Klaeber’s text keeps ‘hēold mec ond hæfde Hrēðel cyning’, and the sense is the same. ‘geaf mē sinc ond symbẹl’ is ‘gave me treasure and feast’ (‘symbel’, the formal banquet, with Klaeber’s dot under the ‘e’): the two gifts of a king, treasure and a place at the table. ‘sibbe gemunde’ is ‘remembered kinship’, ‘gemunan’ with the genitive ‘sibbe’ (‘sibb’, the bond among kin; cf. ‘sibling’).

sentences.t:
næs ic him tō līfe lāðra ōwihte
beorn in burgum þonne his bearna hwylc,
Herebeald ond Hæðcyn oððe Hygelāc mīn.
sentences.l: I was not to him in life at all more hateful, a man in the strongholds, than any of his children, Herebeald and Hæthcyn or Hygelac mine.
sentences.i: All his days I was no more hateful to him, a man in his strongholds, than any of his own sons, Herebeald and Hæthcyn or my Hygelac.
sentences.n: ‘næs ic him lāðra’ is ‘I was not more hateful to him’, with ‘lāðra’ a comparative adjective (nominative singular), ‘ōwihte’ ‘by anything, at all’, and ‘þonne’ introducing the comparison, ‘than any of his children’ (‘his bearna hwylc’, ‘which one of his children’). ‘tō līfe’ is literally ‘for life’, which I take as ‘throughout his life’. The apparatus lists the variants ‘wihte’ and ‘ōwiht’. ‘beorn in burgum’ is ‘a man in the strongholds’. The three sons are Hrethel’s: Herebeald the eldest, Hæthcyn, and Hygelac, ‘mīn’, ‘mine’, a touch of affection from a speaker who is Hygelac’s nephew.

sentences.t:
Wæs þām yldestan ungedēfe
mǣges dǣdum morþọrbed strêd,
syððan hyne Hæðcyn of hornbogan,
his frēawine flāne geswencte,
miste mercelses ond his mǣg ofscēt,
brōðor ōðerne blōdigan gāre.
sentences.l: Was for the eldest unseemly, by a kinsman’s deeds, a murder-bed strewn, after Hæthcyn from a horn-bow, him, his lord-friend, with an arrow struck, missed the mark and his kinsman shot dead, brother the other, with a bloody spear.
sentences.i: For the eldest a bed of murder was spread, unfittingly, by a kinsman’s deed: Hæthcyn, shooting from his horn-bow, struck his own lord and brother with an arrow, missed his mark, and killed his kinsman, one brother the other, with the bloody shaft.
sentences.n: The main clause is ‘Wæs … morþọrbed strêd’, ‘a murder-bed was strewn’ (‘morþor’ ‘murder’ + ‘bed’; the dot under the ‘o’ is the metre sign), for ‘þām yldestan’ (dative, ‘for the eldest’, Herebeald), ‘mǣges dǣdum’ (‘by a kinsman’s deeds’, instrumental). ‘strêd’ is a participle, ‘strewn’, with Klaeber’s circumflex for a contracted vowel. ‘ungedēfe’ is ‘unseemly’; the manuscript has ‘ungedefelice’ and Sievers shortened it, so the form may be adjective or adverb, and I give both senses. The ‘syððan’ clause names the deed: ‘hyne’ (him, Herebeald) is the object of ‘geswencte’ (‘struck, afflicted’); ‘his frēawine’ is ‘his lord-friend’, his elder brother; ‘of hornbogan’ is ‘from a horn-bow’, ‘flāne’ ‘with an arrow’. ‘miste mercelses’ is ‘missed the mark’ (‘mercels’, a rare word whose sense comes from ‘mearc’, ‘mark’: a guess), ‘ofscēt’ ‘shot dead’ and ‘gāre’ (a spear, here the arrow). ‘brōðor ōðerne’ is ‘one brother the other’. Bugge and Trautmann read ‘frēowine’, which would be ‘noble friend’ (‘frēo-’ ‘free, noble’) in place of ‘lord-friend’ (‘frēa-’ ‘lord’).

sentences.t:
Þæt wæs feohlēas gefeoht, fyrenum gesyngad,
hreðre hygemēðe;
sentences.l: That was a fee-less fight, sinned with crimes, in the breast mind-weary;
sentences.i: That was a fight no payment could settle, a sin committed in crime, weary in heart and mind;
sentences.n: ‘feohlēas gefeoht’ is ‘a fee-less fight’ (‘feoh’ ‘cattle, money’ + ‘lēas’ ‘without’): no wergild could be paid, because slayer and slain were both the king’s own sons. ‘fyrenum gesyngad’ is ‘sinned with crimes’ (a past participle of ‘gesyngian’, with ‘fyrenum’ dative plural), which I take to mean that the deed counted as sin though it was unintended. ‘hreðre’ is a dative, ‘in the breast’; ‘hygemēðe’ (‘hyge’ ‘mind’ + ‘mēðe’ ‘weary’) has the nominative singular form of the adjective and no dative ending, so it does not agree with ‘hreðre’ and hangs loosely on the clause, ‘weary of mind’, as vague as the Old English; Trautmann, Holthausen and, with a query, Scheinert read ‘-mēðo’; that changes the ending, and the apparatus does not say how they take it.

sentences.t:
sceolde hwæðre swā þēah
æðeling unwrecen ealdres linnan.
sentences.l: had to, however, even so, the atheling, unavenged, part with life.
sentences.i: Yet for all that the prince had to lose his life unavenged.
sentences.n: ‘sceolde hwæðre swā þēah’ piles three adverbs, ‘however, so, though’, into one emphatic ‘nevertheless’. ‘æðeling’ is Herebeald, ‘unwrecen’ (‘unavenged’, the negative past participle of ‘wrecan’) is predicative, and ‘linnan’ is ‘cease, part with’, taking the genitive ‘ealdres’ (‘of life’); the verb takes either case. Feud law asks that a killing be answered by vengeance or by payment, and here, with the killer his brother, neither can be had by the father.

sentences.l: So it is mournful for an old man to endure, that his son should ride young on the gallows;
sentences.i: So it is a grief to an old man to live to see his son, young as he is, swing on the gallows;
sentences.n: ‘Swā’ opens a comparison: Hrethel’s case is like that of a father in the following picture. ‘bið geōmorlīc … tō gebīdanne’ is ‘it is mournful to endure’, the adjective with the dative ‘gomelum ceorle’ (‘for an old man’; ‘ceorl’ a free man) and ‘tō gebīdanne’ an inflected infinitive, ‘to live to see’ (‘gebīdan’ ‘experience’); ‘bið’ is the gnomic present, true always. The ‘þæt’ clause gives the thing endured: ‘his byre rīde’ (‘his son should ride’, subjunctive of ‘rīdan’) ‘giong on galgan’, ‘young on the gallows’. ‘rīde’ pictures the hanged body as riding the gallows-tree while it swings; the image is harsh and meant to be.

sentences.t:
þonne hē gyd wrece,
sārigne sang, þonne his sunu hangað
hrefne tō hrōðre, ond hē him helpe ne mæg
eald ond infrōd ǣnige gefremman.
sentences.l: when he may utter a lay, a sorrowful song, when his son hangs for the raven as comfort, and he is not able, old and very wise, to do him any help.
sentences.i: when he utters a lament, a song of sorrow, while his son hangs there as comfort for the raven, and he, old and full of years, cannot give him any help.
sentences.n: Two ‘þonne’ clauses hang on the ‘tō gebīdanne’ above. ‘gyd wrece’ is ‘utter a lay’, a subjunctive of ‘wrecan’, with ‘sārigne sang’ (‘sorrowful song’) in variation: the father’s dirge. ‘hangað’ is ‘hangs’ (third person singular), ‘hrefne tō hrōðre’ ‘to the raven for comfort’ (‘hrefne’ dative ‘raven’, ‘hrōðor’ ‘solace, joy’), which I take to mean that the corpse is the raven’s meal; the sense of ‘hrōðre’ is grim and not certain. ‘ond hē him helpe ne mæg … gefremman’ is ‘he cannot render him help’; Klaeber’s italic ‘e’ in ‘helpe’ marks his change, for the manuscript has ‘helpan’ (Kemble’s ‘helpe’ is adopted), and ‘helpe ǣnige’ (accusative, ‘any help’) is the object of ‘gefremman’ (‘perform’). ‘infrōd’ is ‘very old, wise with years’.

sentences.t:
Symble bið gemyndgad morna gehwylce
eaforan ellorsīð;
sentences.l: Always he is reminded, each morning, of the heir’s journey elsewhere;
sentences.i: Every morning, always, he is reminded of his son’s journey away from this world;
sentences.n: ‘Symble’ is ‘always’, ‘bið gemyndgad’ the passive, ‘is reminded’ (‘gemyndgian’ takes the accusative of the thing), and ‘morna gehwylce’ ‘each morning’. The father is not named; he is the unspoken subject carried over from the lines above. ‘eaforan’ is the genitive of ‘eafora’ (‘heir, son’), and ‘ellorsīð’ is ‘elsewhere-journey’ (‘ellor’ ‘elsewhere’ + ‘sīð’ ‘journey’), a delicate word for death, a compound of the kind seen in ‘ellorgāst’, ‘elsewhere-spirit’.

sentences.t:
ōðres ne gȳmeð
tō gebīdanne burgum in innan
yrfeweardas, þonne se ān hafað
þurh dēaðes nȳd dǣda gefondad.
sentences.l: of another he does not care to await in the strongholds, heirs, when the one has through death’s compulsion experienced the deeds.
sentences.i: He has no heart to wait in his strongholds for another heir, once death’s hard need has had its way with the one.
sentences.n: This sentence is the hardest of the passage, and I give a plain reading, not a sure one. ‘ōðres ne gȳmeð’ is ‘he cares not for another’ (‘gȳman’ takes the genitive), and ‘tō gebīdanne … yrfeweardas’ is ‘to await heirs’ (‘yrfeweard’ ‘heir, guardian of the inheritance’), ‘burgum in innan’ ‘in the strongholds’ (dative plural, ‘in innan’ ‘within’). The ‘þonne’ clause reads ‘when the one has, by death’s compulsion, experienced deeds’: ‘se ān’ is the son already dead, ‘þurh dēaðes nȳd’ ‘through death’s need’, and ‘dǣda gefondad’ ‘tried deeds’ (‘gefondian’ ‘experience, find out’), meaning he has undergone what death does. Grundtvig and Müllenhoff move the genitive (‘þurh dǣda nȳd dēaðes gefondad’, ‘through the compulsion of deeds’), and Grundtvig elsewhere and Bugge change ‘nȳd’ to ‘nīð’. The point holds on any reading: one son lost, the father finds no comfort in another.

sentences.t:
Gesyhð sorhcearig on his suna būre
wīnsele wēstne, windge reste
rēte berofene, —
sentences.l: He sees, sorrow-careful, in his son’s bower the wine-hall deserted, the windy resting-place bereft of joy, —
sentences.i: Sorrowing, he sees in his son’s chamber the wine-hall empty, the wind-swept resting-place bereft of joy —
sentences.n: ‘Gesyhð’ is ‘sees’ (‘gesēon’, contracted), the verb of the whole picture, with ‘sorhcearig’ (‘sorrow-careful’) describing the one who sees. The objects stand in apposition: ‘wīnsele wēstne’ (‘wine-hall, deserted’) and ‘windge reste’ (‘windy resting-place’), both accusatives, ‘windge’ agreeing with ‘reste’; the empty bower, open to the wind, is both. ‘on his suna būre’ is ‘in his son’s bower’ (‘būr’ ‘chamber, private room’). ‘rēte berofene’ is ‘bereft of joy’ (‘berofene’ the strong past participle of ‘berēofan’ ‘bereave’, agreeing with ‘reste’). Klaeber’s italic ‘ē’ in ‘rēte’ marks an alteration; the manuscript has ‘reote’; Thorpe read ‘rōte’, Grein (first edition) and Rieger ‘rēoce’, Bugge ‘r(e)ōte’ (‘rest’), Holder ‘rōte’ (‘joy’), and Klaeber follows Holthausen’s later editions, ‘rēte’ (originally ‘rǣte’), so ‘joy’ is a guess at a doubtful word. The dash is Klaeber’s; it turns from what he sees to the cause.

sentences.t:
rīdend swefað,
hæleð in hoðman;
sentences.l: the riders sleep, the heroes in the dark place;
sentences.i: the riders sleep, the warriors lie in the grave;
sentences.n: ‘rīdend’ is a noun made from the present participle of ‘rīdan’, ‘riders’, the mounted warriors of the household; ‘swefað’ is ‘sleep’, the plural present, and ‘sleep’ is the euphemism for dead. ‘hæleð’ (‘heroes’) is in apposition, and ‘in hoðman’ is ‘in the hoðma’, a dative of a weak noun glossed ‘dark place, covert’, which I read as the grave. Grein read ‘swefeð’ (singular), which would make the riders one man. The riders are presumably the dead son’s companions, as the bower is his.

sentences.t:
nis þǣr hearpan swēg,
gomen in geardum, swylce ðǣr iū wǣron.
sentences.l: There is no harp’s sound, mirth in the courts, such as there formerly were.
sentences.i: No harp sounds there, no revelry in the courts, as there used to be.
sentences.n: ‘nis’ is ‘ne is’, ‘is not’; the subjects are ‘hearpan swēg’ (‘the harp’s sound’, ‘hearpan’ genitive) and ‘gomen’ (‘mirth, game’), the latter in apposition. ‘in geardum’ is ‘in the courts’ (dative plural of ‘geard’, ‘yard, enclosure’). ‘swylce ðǣr iū wǣron’ is ‘such as there formerly were’; ‘iū’ is ‘formerly’, and ‘wǣron’ is plural, picking up both harp and mirth. The lines echo the last survivor’s lament in Fitt XXXII (2262, ‘Næs hearpan wyn, gomen glēobēames’): the poet reaches for the same picture, an unplayed harp, for two different griefs. Klaeber prints no closing quotation mark, so Beowulf’s speech runs on.
